definition: What one row of a table or query result represents, such as one row per order or one row per country per month. Stating it before writing GROUP BY prevents most aggregation mistakes.
The rule that SQL evaluates AND before OR, so a filter mixing them groups conditions unexpectedly unless every OR group is wrapped in parentheses.
SQL's logic in which a condition is TRUE, FALSE or NULL (unknown). Any comparison with NULL is unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows whose condition is TRUE.
A NULL-safe comparison that treats NULL as an ordinary value, so rows with NULL are not silently dropped the way they are with the plain not-equal operator.
A function that returns its first non-NULL argument, used to give missing values a display default such as 'none'. Replacing NULL with 0 in averages distorts results.
An expression that returns the result of the first WHEN condition that is TRUE, or the ELSE value; without an ELSE, unmatched rows get NULL.
Dates stored as text in the form 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'. Because the largest unit comes first, alphabetical order equals chronological order, so string comparison works as a date filter.
A period filter that includes its start and excludes the start of the next period, such as order_date >= '2025-11-01' AND order_date < '2025-12-01', so the last day is never cut off.
A SQLite function that converts a date to a fractional number of days. Subtracting two julianday values gives a duration in days; multiplying by 24 gives hours.
The clause that filters groups after aggregation, so it can test values like COUNT(*) or SUM(revenue). Row conditions belong in WHERE, which runs before grouping.
A selected column that is neither grouped nor aggregated. SQLite allows it and fills it from an arbitrary row of each group; PostgreSQL rejects the query.
A standard SQL addition to an aggregate, as in COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE channel = 'web'), that restricts that one aggregate to matching rows inside each group.
A join that keeps every row of the left table and fills the right table's columns with NULL where no match exists. Right-table filters belong in its ON clause.
The row multiplication that happens when a join follows a one-to-many relationship. Values stored on the 'one' side repeat once per match, so summing them inflates totals.
A subquery in the FROM clause that acts like a temporary table with its own grain, often used to aggregate a detailed table before joining it.
A join of a table to itself using two aliases for two roles, such as employee and manager, to follow a link stored within the same table.
A filter that keeps rows having at least one match in another table, written with EXISTS or IN (subquery). Unlike a join, it never duplicates rows.
A filter that keeps rows with no match in another table, written as NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right_key IS NULL. NOT IN fails when the subquery contains NULL.
A subquery that returns exactly one row and one column, such as an overall average, and can be used anywhere a single value is allowed.
A named intermediate result defined with WITH name AS (...). CTEs let a long analysis read as ordered steps, each of which can be run and checked on its own.
A CTE with an anchor query, UNION ALL and a step that joins back to the CTE itself, repeating until no new rows appear. Used to walk hierarchies of any depth.
A function followed by OVER (...) that computes a value from a set of related rows while keeping every row, unlike GROUP BY, which collapses them.
The part of a window definition that splits rows into groups so the window calculation, such as a ranking or running total, restarts for each group.
Window functions that return a value from the previous (LAG) or next (LEAD) row in the window order, used for period-over-period comparisons.
The range of rows around the current row that a window aggregate sees, such as ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for a 7-row moving average.
A sequence of steps, such as session, add to cart and purchase, reported as counts and step-to-step conversion rates to show where people drop off.
The share of a group of customers who started in the same period, such as their first-order month, who are active again a given number of periods later.
A query that returns the rows breaking a stated rule, such as orphaned references or impossible dates, so an empty result means the rule holds.
The database's description of how it will execute a query, shown in SQLite with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN. SEARCH means an index narrowed the work; SCAN means every row was read.
Describes a condition the database can answer with an index, typically a bare column compared with a constant. Wrapping the column in a function usually makes it non-sargable.
